final_proof:
Let m ∈ M. Since M is locally Euclidean of dimension d, there are an open neighborhood V of m, an open set O ⊆ ℝ^d, and a homeomorphism φ: V → O.

Put x = φ(m). Because O is open and contains x, there exists r > 0 such that the Euclidean open ball B(x,r) is contained in O. For each positive integer n, define

U_n = φ⁻¹(B(x,r/n)).

Each U_n is open in V, hence open in M because V is open in M, and m ∈ U_n. The restriction φ|_{U_n}: U_n → B(x,r/n) is a homeomorphism: this follows by restricting φ and its continuous inverse to the indicated subspaces. Thus every U_n is homeomorphic to an open ball in ℝ^d; equivalently, U_n is the image of that ball under (φ|_{U_n})⁻¹.

We now verify the local-basis property. Let N be any neighborhood of m. By the definition of neighborhood, there is an open set G in M such that m ∈ G ⊆ N. Then G ∩ V is open in V and contains m. Since φ is a homeomorphism, φ(G ∩ V) is an open subset of ℝ^d containing x. Therefore there is ε > 0 such that B(x,ε) ⊆ φ(G ∩ V). By the Archimedean property, choose a positive integer n with n > r/ε, so that r/n < ε. It follows that

U_n = φ⁻¹(B(x,r/n)) ⊆ φ⁻¹(B(x,ε)) ⊆ G ∩ V ⊆ N.

Thus every neighborhood N of m contains some U_n. Hence {U_n : n ≥ 1} is a countable local basis at m, and each of its members is homeomorphic to an open ball in ℝ^d.

This also covers d = 0: ℝ^0 is a singleton, every positive-radius ball in it is that singleton, and the construction merely repeats the same valid basis neighborhood.
